name: Paulus Alvarus
otherNames: Paulus Alvarus of Cordoba; Alvarus Cordubensis, the Latin name in the headings of his works
Alvarus Paulus, as he calls himself in most of his letters, Nicolás Antonio notes
Aurelius Flavius, the names his correspondents gave him
knownFor: A Christian layman of Cordoba under the Muslim emirs, the closest friend of Eulogius of Cordoba and the writer of his Life. His letters and poems survive, and the Luminous Index of 854, a defense of the Cordoban martyrs, is believed to be his.
dates: A letter of his to Eleazar names era 878, AD 840, as the year now running. The Luminous Index gives 854, era 892. He wrote the Life of Eulogius after Eulogius's death on Saturday, 11 March, in 859 by the reckoning of Ambrosio de Morales. Nicolás Antonio says nothing certain is known of his own death. A note to Antonio's notice cites Enrique Flórez, author of the España Sagrada, for about 861 (the scan reads $61). A chronicle under the name of Luitprand, which Antonio calls a pseudo-Luitprand, gives 4 May, era 907, AD 869, and Antonio rejects it. No source gives his birth
place: Cordoba, the city named in the headings of his works, where Eulogius found Aurelius at his house
role: Layman and writer; biographer of Eulogius of Cordoba, who calls him a teacher praised across the West for his knowledge of Scripture

keyWorks.title: Life and Passion of Eulogius (Vita vel passio sancti Eulogii)
keyWorks.about: written by his closest friend for the yearly feast, after the burial. Alvarus promises to tell only what he saw and tested himself. It is the one witness to Eulogius's election to Toledo, a note in Lorenzana's edition says. Nicolás Antonio lists with it a hymn for the feast and an epitaph

keyWorks.title: Letters (Liber epistolarum)
keyWorks.about: to John of Seville on Christ's nature, recalling the days when the teaching of Elipandus of Toledo laid waste his province; to Abbot Speraindeo; to Bishop Saul, after an illness in which, near death, he asked for penance; and to Eleazar, a Christian who had become a Jew. Antonio says Saul refused to absolve him and hinted that he had sided with a false bishop. A later owner of the codex struck out and cut away parts of Eleazar's own letters, Antonio says

keyWorks.title: Luminous Index (Indiculus luminosus)
keyWorks.about: dated 854. It defends the Christians of Cordoba who offered themselves for martyrdom unasked, and reads prophecies as pointing to Muhammad. Its author grieves that young Christians read Arabic books eagerly and that hardly one in a thousand can write a decent letter of greeting to a brother. A promised second book is lacking. It is unsigned and believed to be his

traces: A codex of the church of Cordoba, in Gothic script, kept his works, and Morales saw it. Thomas Tamayo de Vargas, the royal chronicler, praised another at Toledo. Antonio's own copy came from one in Cardinal Barberini's library at Rome. Tamayo de Vargas had given it to the cardinal at Madrid.
His Life of Eulogius was printed by Morales and then by Andreas Schott. Notes in Migne's edition cite his letters from Enrique Flórez's España Sagrada, volume XI.
The editors of Alcuin's works cite his letter to John of Seville as a witness that Elipandus drew some Cordobans into his teaching.
remembered: Eulogius calls him his teacher, praised across the West for his knowledge of Scripture, and a fountain of wisdom in their time.

A chronicle under Luitprand's name called him a holy man of Cordoba, and Juan Tamayo entered him as a saint in the Spanish Martyrology. Antonio, who calls that chronicle a pseudo-Luitprand, dismisses this as Toledo's saint-making.

An old marginal note headed ALVARUS, in an Escorial manuscript of Isidore of Seville's Etymologies, remarks on the nine orders of angels. A note to Antonio's notice reports it and thinks it may come from him.

uncertain: His own life is thin. Beyond his writings, it rests on a few lines in his letters and on Eulogius, his closest friend. Antonio finds nothing certain about his death.

His ancestry. In a letter to Eleazar he calls himself a Hebrew by faith and by race, whose forebears came from Abraham. Antonio accepts that, if the letter is really his. In another letter Alvarus quotes lines on the fearless Getae, which he gives to Virgil; a note in the edition says they are not Virgil's. Antonio reads the lines as a claim to be a Goth, perhaps in jest. Antonio leaves both open. Morales thought him of noble birth because Eulogius greets him as Serenity; Antonio notes that such titles were ordinary courtesy then.

His marriage. Antonio reads a greeting to his household, in a letter from John of Seville, as a hint that he was married. Morales's notice says he was married, as far as one can guess. A note in Lorenzana's edition of Eulogius reports that Morales, Antonio and Flórez believed so, and calls their arguments weak.

The Luminous Index. It is unsigned. Morales first denied it to Alvarus, because it never names Eulogius, then gave it to him in his History. Antonio agrees, from its style and date and from the Life's mention of a book by Alvarus on the persecution. The chronicles that Antonio ties to Hieronymus Romanus de la Higuera gave it to Bonitus or to Wistremir, bishops of Toledo.
The Book of Sparks (Liber scintillarum). A codex at Sahagún gives it to Alvarus of Cordoba. A note to Antonio's notice reports other manuscripts that give it to Bede, to Defensor or to Cassiodorus.
His death. Antonio says nothing certain is known. A note to his notice cites Flórez for about 861 (the scan reads $61). The pseudo-Luitprand gives 4 May 869, and Antonio rejects it.
Eleazar. Antonio calls him a man from Gaul, Hebrew by faith after being a Christian. The sources say no more of who he was.

Eulogius's brother. Eulogius writes of his brothers Alvarus and Isidore, exiled in the lands of Louis, king of Bavaria. Juan Tamayo, author of a Spanish Martyrology, took this Alvarus to be Paulus Alvarus, and called the brothers bound by a shared life rather than by blood. Nicolás Antonio holds that this Alvarus was another man, Eulogius's brother by birth, and that Paulus's bond with Eulogius was friendship.
Who buried Eulogius. Alvarus says the Christians bought back the head the next day and buried the body at St Zoilus on the third day. He does not say he buried his friend himself.
